```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4
)
```

Peak finding in chromatographR places an apex wherever the first derivative of
the signal changes from positive to negative. Noise makes the derivative change
sign at every small wiggle, so `find_peaks()` smooths the signal first;
`smooth_window` sets the width of that smoothing, in timepoints.

Three filters are available to remove small or spurious peaks:
`min_amplitude`, `min_curvature` and `min_prominence_snr`. The first two are in
the instrument's units. The third discards apices that rise less than that many
noise standard deviations above the higher of the two valleys beside them. All
three default to `0`.

This article covers `smooth_window` and `min_prominence_snr`. The prominence
filter is the only one measured against the noise, so one value can serve
across datasets. It needs baseline-corrected data, though: `find_peaks()`
estimates the noise from the timepoints outside peaks, and baseline drift
inflates that estimate. Too narrow a window can also make it discard real
peaks. See [`find_peaks`](../reference/find_peaks.html) for the other two
filters.

The recommended workflow is:

1. Measure your peak widths.
2. Set `smooth_window` to about a third of a typical width.
3. Use [`filter_peaks()`](../reference/filter_peaks.html) to remove detections
   narrower or wider than any real peak.

The sections below test that advice on simulated traces whose true peaks are
known, and the last applies it to the example data `Sa_pr`.

```{r setup}
library(chromatographR)
```

## A trace with known peaks

The next three sections use a simulated trace: nine gaussian peaks, each 28
timepoints wide at half height, with heights from 1000 down to 3 against noise
of standard deviation 1.

```{r trace, fig.height = 4}
#| fig-cap: "The simulated trace, with each peak labelled by its signal-to-noise ratio. The inset zooms in on the five smallest peaks, with heights of 20 down to 3, which sit close to the noise."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Simulate the trace"
set.seed(1)
tt  <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.01)
ctr <- c(3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27)
hgt <- c(1000, 300, 100, 40, 20, 12, 8, 5, 3)
y   <- rep(0, length(tt))
for (i in seq_along(ctr)) {
  y <- y + hgt[i] * exp(-(tt - ctr[i])^2 / (2 * 0.12^2))
}
y <- y + rnorm(length(tt))

small <- hgt <= 20
zoom  <- list(x = c(14, 29.5), y = c(-4, 26))

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(tt, y, type = "n", xlab = "Time", ylab = "Signal")
rect(zoom$x[1], -25, zoom$x[2], 45, col = "grey96", border = NA)
lines(tt, y, col = "grey55")
text(ctr[!small], hgt[!small], paste("SNR", hgt[!small]), pos = 4,
     offset = 0.2, cex = 0.65, col = "firebrick2")

inset <- c(grconvertX(c(13.5, 30), "user", "ndc"),
           grconvertY(c(230, 1000), "user", "ndc"))
par(fig = inset, new = TRUE, mar = c(1.6, 1.8, 0.3, 0.3), cex.axis = 0.65,
    mgp = c(3, 0.4, 0), tcl = -0.2)
plot(tt, y, type = "n", xlim = zoom$x, ylim = zoom$y, xlab = "", ylab = "")
rect(par("usr")[1], par("usr")[3], par("usr")[2], par("usr")[4],
     col = "grey96", border = NA)
lines(tt, y, col = "grey55")
box()
text(ctr[small], hgt[small], paste("SNR", hgt[small]), pos = 4,
     offset = 0.2, cex = 0.6, col = "firebrick2")
```

An apex counts as found when it lands within 0.05 of a true center, and as
spurious otherwise. The grid runs `find_peaks()` at nine windows and three
prominence thresholds:

```{r score-helper}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Scoring function"
score <- function(p, tol = 0.05){
  if (!nrow(p)) return(c(found = 0, spurious = 0))
  d <- tt[p$pos]
  c(found    = sum(vapply(ctr, function(c0) any(abs(d - c0) <= tol), logical(1))),
    spurious = sum(!vapply(d, function(x) any(abs(ctr - x) <= tol), logical(1))))
}
found_at    <- function(w, k) with(res, found[smooth_window == w & min_prominence_snr == k])
spurious_at <- function(w, k) with(res, spurious[smooth_window == w & min_prominence_snr == k])
first_all   <- function(k) with(res, min(smooth_window[min_prominence_snr == k & found == 9]))
```

```{r score}
#| warning: false
windows <- c(1, 3, 6, 10, 12, 20, 28, 40, 60)
snrs    <- c(0, 3, 5)
grid    <- expand.grid(smooth_window = windows, min_prominence_snr = snrs)
scored  <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(w, k) {
  p <- find_peaks(y, smooth_window = w, min_prominence_snr = k)
  score(p)
}, grid$smooth_window, grid$min_prominence_snr))
res <- cbind(grid, scored)
```

The counts are plotted at the end of the next section. At the three narrowest
windows, which are under a third of the peak width, `find_peaks()` also warns
that the window is too narrow; those warnings are hidden on this page.

## Narrow windows let noise through and split real peaks

Noise can split a small peak into several apices, each rising only a little
above the notch beside it, so `min_prominence_snr` discards the pieces along
with the noise and the peak is lost. To see this, wrap the trace as a
one-sample chromatogram and pass it to `get_peaks()` at windows of 3 and 10
timepoints, with `min_prominence_snr = 3`:

```{r narrow-fit}
#| warning: false
sim <- list(sim = matrix(y, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(tt, "1")))
narrow <- lapply(c(3, 10), function(w)
  get_peaks(sim, lambdas = "1", fit = "gaussian", smooth_window = w,
            min_prominence_snr = 3, cl = 1, show_progress = FALSE))
```

```{r narrow-count, include = FALSE}
n_fitted <- sapply(narrow, function(p) {
  rt <- data.frame(p[[1]][["1"]])$rt
  sum(vapply(c(15, 18, 21), function(c0) any(abs(rt - c0) < 0.05), logical(1)))
})
apices3 <- find_peaks(y, smooth_window = 3, bounds = TRUE)
fragments <- function(c0) apices3[abs(tt[apices3$pos] - c0) <= 0.15, ]
```

```{r narrow-plot, fig.height = 5}
#| fig-cap: "Peaks fitted between 14 and 22 minutes at windows of 3 (top) and 10 (bottom) timepoints, with `min_prominence_snr = 3`. Filled points mark apices that pass the prominence filter, crosses those it removes."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot the fitted peaks and the apices"
#| warning: false
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2.5, 4, 2, 1))
for (i in 1:2) {
  w    <- c(3, 10)[i]
  all  <- find_peaks(y, smooth_window = w)$pos
  kept <- find_peaks(y, smooth_window = w, min_prominence_snr = 3)$pos
  gone <- setdiff(all, kept)
  plot(narrow[[i]], chrom_list = sim, xlim = c(14, 22), ylim = c(-3, 23),
       main = sprintf("smooth_window = %d, min_prominence_snr = 3", w))
  points(tt[kept], y[kept], pch = 21, cex = 1, bg = "royalblue", col = "white")
  points(tt[gone], y[gone], pch = 4, cex = 0.8, lwd = 1.5, col = "darkorange2")
}
legend("topright", c("apex kept", "apex removed by the filter"),
       pch = c(21, 4), pt.bg = c("royalblue", NA), col = c("white", "darkorange2"),
       pt.lwd = c(1, 1.5), bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
```

Between 14 and 22 minutes the 3-timepoint window fits
`r n_fitted[1]` of the three peaks. Noise splits the SNR-20 peak into
`r nrow(fragments(15))` apices and the SNR-12 peak into
`r nrow(fragments(18))`, each rising at most
`r round(max(fragments(15)$prominence, fragments(18)$prominence), 1)` above
the notch beside it. Every fragment falls below the threshold of 3, so the
filter removes them all and nothing is left to fit. The 10-timepoint window
keeps each summit in one piece and fits all `r n_fitted[2]`. At either window a
few noise apices also clear the threshold.

The same happens to every small peak on the trace. The table gives, for each
true peak, the number of apices within 0.05 of its center and the largest of
their prominences:

```{r split-helper}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Prominence of the apices near each true peak"
peak_prominence <- function(w){
  p <- find_peaks(y, smooth_window = w, bounds = TRUE)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(ctr, function(c0){
    near <- which(abs(tt[p$pos] - c0) <= 0.05)
    if (!length(near)) return(c(apices = 0, prominence = NA))
    c(apices = length(near), prominence = max(p$prominence[near]))
  }))
}
```

```{r split}
summits <- data.frame(height = hgt, w3 = peak_prominence(3),
                      w28 = peak_prominence(28))
summits
```

```{r split-values, include = FALSE}
notched <- summits$w3.prominence[summits$w3.apices > 1]
```

The four tallest peaks keep one apex and their full prominence at either
window. At 3 timepoints the five small ones split in two, and their prominence
falls to between `r round(min(notched), 1)` and `r round(max(notched), 1)`,
against a noise level of about 1. Height does not decide which of them
survive: the SNR-3 peak keeps a prominence of
`r round(summits$w3.prominence[summits$height == 3], 1)`, while the SNR-12 peak
falls to `r round(summits$w3.prominence[summits$height == 12], 1)`.

Across every window in the grid, the counts show the trade-off. Without the
prominence filter, spurious apices fall from `r spurious_at(1, 0)` at a
one-timepoint window to `r spurious_at(60, 0)` at 60, and all nine real peaks
survive every window.

```{r smoothing, fig.height = 3.6}
#| fig-cap: "Spurious apices (left) and real peaks found (right) at each window, for three prominence thresholds. The dashed vertical line marks the recommended window, a third of the peak width. Zero counts are drawn at 0.75 so that they show on the log scale."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot the counts"
cols <- c("grey25", "firebrick2", "steelblue3")
advised <- 2.355 * 0.12 / 0.01 / 3
spur <- matrix(res$spurious, nrow = length(windows))
fnd  <- matrix(res$found,    nrow = length(windows))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.4, 1))
matplot(windows, pmax(spur, 0.75), type = "b", log = "y", col = cols,
        pch = 16, lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        xlab = "smooth_window (timepoints)", ylab = "Count (log scale)",
        main = "Spurious apices")
abline(v = advised, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("topright", c(paste("min_prominence_snr =", snrs), "a third of the FWHM"),
       col = c(cols, "grey50"), lwd = c(2, 2, 2, 1), lty = c(1, 1, 1, 2),
       bty = "n", cex = 0.72)
matplot(windows, fnd, type = "b", col = cols, pch = 16, lty = 1, lwd = 2,
        xlab = "smooth_window (timepoints)", ylab = "Peaks (out of 9)",
        main = "Real peaks found")
abline(v = advised, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
abline(h = 9, lty = 2, col = "grey60")
```

The filter removes spurious apices at any window, but at narrow windows it
removes real peaks too. At 3 timepoints, `min_prominence_snr = 3` finds
`r found_at(3, 3)` of the nine and `= 5` finds `r found_at(3, 5)`. To keep all
nine, `= 3` needs a window of `r first_all(3)` timepoints and `= 5` needs
`r first_all(5)`. At 10 timepoints, about a third of the peak width, `= 3`
keeps all nine and cuts the spurious apices from `r spurious_at(10, 0)` to
`r spurious_at(10, 3)`.

## Filtering the noise that remains

At the recommended window, `min_prominence_snr = 3` still leaves many small 
noisy peaks among the real ones. These can be removed after fitting using
`filter_peaks()` using various criteria. The table below counts the
fitted peaks that each criterion retains, using the 10-timepoint peak table 
derived from the 10-timepoint smoothing window:

```{r noise-helper}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Count the real and spurious fits"
fit10 <- narrow[[2]]
count_fits <- function(p) {
  rt   <- data.frame(p[[1]][["1"]])$rt
  real <- vapply(rt, function(r) any(abs(ctr - r) <= 0.05), logical(1))
  setNames(c(sum(real), sum(!real)),
           c(sprintf("real (of %d)", length(ctr)), "spurious"))
}
fits10 <- data.frame(fit10[[1]][["1"]])
fits10$real <- vapply(fits10$rt, function(r) any(abs(ctr - r) <= 0.05), logical(1))
r2_fit10 <- fit10
r2_fit10[[1]][["1"]] <- fit10[[1]][["1"]][fits10$r.squared >= 0.8, ]
```

```{r noise-filters}
rbind(
  "none"                   = count_fits(fit10),
  "min_fwhm = 0.1"         = count_fits(filter_peaks(fit10, min_fwhm = 0.1)),
  "window_limited = FALSE" = count_fits(filter_peaks(fit10, window_limited = FALSE)),
  "min_height = 5"         = count_fits(filter_peaks(fit10, min_height = 5)),
  "converged = TRUE"       = count_fits(filter_peaks(fit10, converged = TRUE)),
  "r.squared >= 0.8"       = count_fits(r2_fit10)
)
```

Width separates noise from peaks best. The spurious fits are at most
`r round(max(fits10$FWHM[!fits10$real]), 3)` minutes wide and the real peaks at
least `r round(min(fits10$FWHM[fits10$real]), 2)`, so `min_fwhm = 0.1` removes
all the noise and keeps all nine peaks. The other criteria do worse:

- `window_limited = FALSE` removes only the fits pinned at one timepoint, the
  narrowest width a fit can report.
- `min_height` is in instrument units, and any cutoff that removes the noise
  here also removes the smallest real peak.
- An `r.squared` cutoff removes the noise but also the two smallest real peaks,
  whose fits are noisy.
- `converged` doesn't separate them at all.

## Wide windows merge close peaks

A window that is too narrow fills the peak list with noise, which is easy to
see. A window that is too wide can merge neighboring peaks with no warning. In
the figure below, two overlapping peaks are shown whose apices sit 0.30 minutes
apart (about one peak width).

```{r merge-setup}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Simulate the pair and fit it"
set.seed(1)
t2 <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.01)
y2 <- 100 * exp(-(t2 - 4.85)^2 / (2 * 0.12^2)) +
      100 * exp(-(t2 - 5.15)^2 / (2 * 0.12^2)) + rnorm(length(t2))
m2 <- matrix(y2, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(t2, "210"))

tidy_fit <- function(w) {
  fp   <- fit_peaks(m2, lambda = "210", smooth_window = w, fit = "gaussian")
  near <- fp[abs(fp$rt - 500) < 60 & fp$height > 50, ]
  data.frame(smooth_window = w, peaks = nrow(near), widest_FWHM = round(max(near$FWHM)),
             lowest_r.squared = round(min(near$r.squared), 2))
}
```

```{r wide-plot, fig.height = 5}
#| fig-cap: "Two peaks 0.30 apart, fitted at windows of 10 (top) and 28 (bottom) timepoints."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Fit and plot the pair at both windows"
#| warning: false
pair <- list(pair = matrix(y2, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(t2, "1")))
par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(2.5, 4, 2, 1))
for (w in c(10, 28)) {
  pks_pair <- get_peaks(pair, lambdas = "1", fit = "gaussian",
                        smooth_window = w, cl = 1, show_progress = FALSE)
  plot(pks_pair, chrom_list = pair, targets = 5, tol = 0.4,
       main = paste("smooth_window =", w))
}
```

With a 10-point smoothing window, the two fitted shapes follow the trace. With a
28-point smoothing window, a single broad shape is fitted to the whole region,
missing both summits. The fitted values show the same thing, at two more window
sizes. Each row gives the number of fitted peaks that are at least half the 
true height, the widest of their FWHMs (each true peak is
`r round(2.355 * 0.12 / 0.01)` timepoints wide), and the lowest `r.squared`:

```{r merge}
merged <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(3, 10, 28, 40), tidy_fit))
merged
```

Windows of 3 and 10 fit both peaks. At windows of 28 and 40, `fit_peaks()`
reports one peak where there are two. The fit still looks good, with an
`r.squared` of `r merged$lowest_r.squared[merged$smooth_window == 28]`, but its
`FWHM` of `r merged$widest_FWHM[merged$smooth_window == 28]` timepoints is
nearly twice the true width of `r round(2.355 * 0.12 / 0.01)`.

## Application to real data

```{r widths}
data(Sa_pr)
pks    <- get_peaks(Sa_pr, lambdas = 210, cl = 1, show_progress = FALSE)
widths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(pks, function(x) data.frame(x[["210"]])))
dt     <- get_time_resolution(Sa_pr, unit = "min")
median(widths$FWHM, na.rm = TRUE) / dt
```

`FWHM` is in minutes but `smooth_window` counts timepoints, so the last line
divides by the sampling interval: a typical `Sa_pr` peak spans
`r round(median(widths$FWHM, na.rm = TRUE) / dt)` timepoints, which puts
`smooth_window` at about
`r max(1, round(median(widths$FWHM, na.rm = TRUE) / dt / 3))`. Real widths are
messy at both ends (here the narrowest detections are one-timepoint noise fits
and the widest are low, broad humps), so plot the extremes before setting
`min_fwhm` and `max_fwhm`, and don't take them from quantiles.
